| D-185 | **An unverified address could carry a membership into somebody else's organisation, and a lifted DNC suppression left no record of the number** | Two seams from the 17 Aug audits (S-2, S-4), plus the four docs-truth findings that were ours (F-8, F-9, F-10, F-12). **S-2 is NOT closed by D-177**, which is the finding's own claim and it is wrong: the report located "`users.email` is an authorization input with no verification check" in `core/clerk_identity.py`, D-177 deleted that file, and the PROPERTY the vendor was assumed to supply was never replaced. `authn/invitations._find_or_create_user` wrote `email_verified_at = now()` on the premise that possession of the emailed token proves the mailbox — but `InvitationCreatedOut.token` hands the raw token to the INVITER, because the client realm has no invitation mailer. So: an owner of any tenant invites an address they do not control, reads the token out of their own 201, redeems it, and holds the only `users` row that address can ever have (`uq_users_email_lower`) with a password they chose. When the real organisation later invites the real person, redemption reused that row, correctly declined to overwrite the password, and attached the membership — up to and including `owner`. The client realm has no second factor (`MFA_REQUIRED_REALMS` is `{'admin'}`), so a password is the whole credential. **Fixed**: the address starts UNVERIFIED (an `email_verify` OTP round trip is what fills the column, and that path was already built and already mailed), and an account that already carries a credential may only take on a NEW membership once its address is proven. A first-time invitee is untouched; the refusal lands before the CAS so the token stays redeemable afterwards. `tests/authn_invitation_verification_test.py` drives all four steps. **S-4**: `DELETE /v1/dnc/{id}` hard-deleted, and the audit row correctly carried no number, so nothing anywhere recorded which number stopped being suppressed. `remove_entry`/`remove_global_entry` now return a `Removal` carrying `compliance.export.subject_ref` — the same one-way handle `deletion_requests.subject_ref` stores — and the routes put it in the audit summary. **A tombstoned ROW was rejected and the reasons are in `dnc.Removal`**: it keeps a number that no longer suppresses anybody (`ERASURE_LIMITATIONS` justifies retaining a DNC entry solely because removing it would make the person callable again, which is false of a released row — so it would be retained personal data with no purpose, DPDP §8(7)); `add_numbers`' dedupe would read the tombstone and report a re-add as `already_suppressed`, which is the one direction hard rule 5 cannot fail in; and it would require the `(tenant_id, phone_e164)` unique key that `check_compliance_invariants` treats as an invariant to become partial. **Docs**: SEC-COMP §4 stops claiming a live client-facing retention misstatement (the DPA delegates to `/legal/privacy` §9, which publishes the seed's numbers, which is what the sweep enforces — §4's own table is the only outlier, and the founder decision stays open); DEV-SETUP names test files that exist; FLOWS §6 states the recording copy's real 30s/120s ladder; and D-95's "`.env` drops to 6" is corrected to a count of `BOOTSTRAP_KEYS` rather than of lines. | **WHY THE SMALLER FIX.** The complete answer to S-2 is to stop returning the invitation token to its issuer and email it instead, which restores the premise and closes the squat as well as the hijack. That needs the invitation mail template and the owner-facing screen that displays the token — `apps/workers/` and `apps/web/`, both outside this change — so what ships here turns an ACCOUNT TAKEOVER into a DENIAL OF SERVICE and says so rather than claiming a closure. `tests/authn_invitation_verification_test.py::test_the_squat_itself_is_still_possible_and_that_is_recorded_here` pins the residual and fails when it goes, which is what closes this entry. **WHY NOT A SIGN-IN GATE.** Refusing a session to an unverified client subject is the more obvious control and is unreachable from here: the verify endpoint needs a session, so it would lock out the very people it is for, and the gate itself belongs in `core/auth.py`. The membership boundary is the one place the escalation actually crosses. **WHAT IS ASSUMED, NOT VERIFIED**: that no path other than invitation redemption writes `users` — proven by grep (one `INSERT INTO users` in `apps/`, `scripts/` and `alembic/` outside test fixtures) and by `POST /v1/auth/signup` requiring `current_identity`, not by an exhaustive audit of every future writer. **COST**: one person joining a second client business now has an extra step, and it is a screen that already exists. |
| D-186 | **A metered call could be counted into the wrong IST month, a late call from a closed month wiped the open month's spend counters, the margin panel priced the whole self-serve motion as a pure loss, and the live spend counter priced a month by a different rule than the invoice** | Five money defects from a deep dive aimed away from the core `docs/evidence/audit-correctness.md` already cleared (`docs/evidence/deepdive-money.md` has the reproductions). **(1) A SECOND SPELLING OF THE BILLING MONTH.** `apps/workers/pipeline.py::_ist_month` was `(moment + timedelta(hours=5, minutes=30)).strftime("%Y-%m")`, correct only for a moment expressed in UTC — `strftime` renders the value's own naive fields rather than converting — and NOTHING guarantees UTC: both adapters parse `ended_at` with `datetime.fromisoformat` and PRESERVE the offset the vendor sent (`engine/bolna.py::_parse_dt`; its `replace(tzinfo=UTC)` covers naive values only), and the vendor is an Indian voice platform. Measured: a call stamped `2026-08-31T23:00+05:30` metered into `2026-09` while its own `usage_events` rows — read back through `billing.service._IST_MONTH`, which goes via `timestamptz` and is correct — sat in `2026-08`. `billing/plans.py::ist_billing_month` was already the stated home of that shift, converts properly for any aware instant and REFUSES a naive one; `_ist_month` is deleted and `_meter` calls it. `tests/one_billing_month_spelling_test.py` is an AST scan asserting that exactly ONE module in `apps/`, `packages/shared/src/` and `scripts/` turns an instant into a `%Y-%m` string. **(2) A CLOSED MONTH'S CALL RESET THE OPEN MONTH.** The `spend_state` upsert's accumulator was `CASE WHEN month = EXCLUDED.month THEN accumulate ELSE EXCLUDED.value END` — right forwards, destructive backwards. A call that settles late (the reconciliation poller's 30-minute window straddling midnight IST on the 1st, an ARQ retry ladder crossing it, a vendor that prices a call minutes after disconnect) arrives with last month's stamp and REPLACED this month's minutes, supplier spend, billed rupees and `capped` flag with its own, stamping `month` backwards — after which `compliance.spend_capped` reads the stale month as no cap at all and the client's panel reads ₹0.00 spent beside minutes correctly read from the ledger. The three near-identical accumulator strings collapse into one `_accumulate(column)` with a three-way rule (same month accumulates, later replaces, EARLIER leaves the counters alone) plus `month = GREATEST(...)`. The call's money is not lost: `usage_events` is the ledger every invoice reads; what a closed month's call may not do is move a ceiling for a month it does not belong to, and `spend_state` holds exactly one month by construction. **(3) THE MARGIN PANEL DID NOT KNOW WHAT A PREPAID CLIENT PAYS.** `margin_for_tenant` computed `revenue = monthly_fee + overage_cost`, which is the managed invoice's subtotal and is ₹0.00 for a `self_serve`/`trial` tenant, who has no `plans` row at all — so the one screen that answers "is this client making us money" reported ₹0.00 revenue against the real supplier cost for the entire self-serve motion, with `margin_pct` suppressed to `None` because that branch reads `revenue > 0`. New `calling_revenue_inr` is the one home of "this period's calling, priced to the client"; `_spend_used`'s prepaid branch (which was right) moved into it and the margin panel reads it. **(4) THE COUNTER AND THE INVOICE PRICED A MONTH DIFFERENTLY.** `usage_summary` spends the included allowance on the DEARER rung first (`split_overage`, deliberately client-favourable); `_billed_for_this_call` spent it in ARRIVAL order at each call's own rung. The two agree for a plan quoting ONE rate, which is every plan today, and diverge as soon as `plans.overage_rate_value` is quoted — measured at ₹880.00 against ₹520.00 on a two-rung month whose cheap minutes arrived first. `/c/<slug>/usage` prints BOTH figures in adjacent cards for one month, and the client's own spend cap is compared against the larger, so their stop button stops them before their bill justifies it. New `billing.service.priced_overage` is the one month-pricing rule (`usage_summary` and `build_invoice` already shared its parts); `overage_increment_inr` charges a call the difference it makes to it, from the per-rung SECONDS the ledger holds. `client_billed_inr` loses its managed branch and becomes `prepaid_billed_inr`; its two managed arguments move to `priced_overage` with the branch. **(5) THE SQL MONTH DEPENDED ON THE SESSION'S `TimeZone`.** `billing.service._IST_MONTH` — interpolated into every query that buckets `usage_events` by month, `ai_quota`'s two included — was `to_char(occurred_at + interval '5 hours 30 minutes', ...)`, and `to_char` on a `timestamptz` renders in the SESSION's `TimeZone`: shifting first and formatting second is the IST month only while that setting is UTC. Measured on one instant (23:00 IST on 31 August) across three zones, `+ interval` answers 2026-08 / **2026-09** / 2026-08 while `AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'` answers 2026-08 three times. Now the latter, with the named zone rather than a literal `+05:30` for the reason the Python side documents its fixed offset. | **THE INCREMENT IS A DIFFERENCE OF TWO MONTH TOTALS, NOT A FORMULA, AND THAT IS THE INVENTION THIS ROW HAS TO DEFEND.** Two properties follow that nothing cheaper has: the increments TELESCOPE (each call's `before` is the previous call's `after`, both computed by one function from one raw-seconds state), so `spend_state.billed_inr` is exactly the month's own overage cost however many calls meter and in whatever order; and a rung's delta may legitimately be NEGATIVE (adding premium minutes moves the allowance onto the premium rung and INCREASES the value rung's overage), so only the month total is a meaningful quantity — pricing the rungs' deltas separately would have had to drop or clamp the negative one and would have been wrong by that amount. It reads SECONDS rather than the quantized minutes because `allocate_paise` distributes a remainder across the whole set and is not linear in any one bucket, so subtracting from minutes would not reproduce the state the previous call priced against. **COST, STATED**: one extra grouped aggregate over the month's `usage_events` per metered call, under a lock `_meter` already holds. **WHY THE ALARM CHANGED WITH (2)**: D-183's crossing arithmetic derives `before` as `after - this call's delta`, and a call that moved nothing has a delta of zero — so the statement had to say whether it applied. `EXCLUDED` is NOT referencable from a `RETURNING` clause (measured against this pg16: `invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "excluded"`, not recalled), so `RETURNING` carries the row's `month` instead and, because `GREATEST` never moves it backwards, `returned_month == :month` IS "this call's totals went in" — one rule, in the statement, read back from the statement. A skipped call gets an INFO line naming both months rather than an `alert()`: around a month boundary this is the expected outcome and an alarm that fires every rollover is a muted one. **PROVEN vs REASONED**: all five reproduce by execution against this tree and this database, each with a test that fails on the pre-fix tree (verified by reverting `apps/workers/pipeline.py` and re-running) — `tests/billing_month_ordering_test.py`, `tests/margin_prepaid_revenue_test.py`, `tests/two_rung_counter_agrees_test.py`. **NOT FIXED, AND WHY**: the client usage card's "Total so far" is `monthly_fee + overage_cost` and omits both one-time charges (the onboarding setup fee, which the invoice prints on that month) and GST, so it is neither the pre-tax usage subtotal nor the invoice total — what it should be is a founder decision about that card, not a refactor, and the invoice is one click away on the adjacent screen. A PREPAID tenant's invoice also shows no line for the minutes their wallet was debited for, because `build_invoice` derives everything from `plans` columns they do not have; what a prepaid statement is (top-ups received? consumption? where GST attaches on a prepaid credit) is a founder-and-accountant decision, and the named external blocker is the same GST registration Rule 46(b) is already waiting on. |
| D-187 | **Two silent premises at the engine seam: the poller believed a summary, and `end_call` had no contract to disagree with** | Three fixes from the voice-path deep dive (`docs/evidence/deepdive-voice.md`). **(1) `_pipeline_settled` read what a call was OWED off a `list_executions` row.** `_expected_artifacts` turns an absence in the engine's record into "nothing was owed" — sound for `get_execution`, unproven for a listing row, which the contract itself calls a summary (`VoiceEngine.get_execution`: "the poller's listing rows are summaries"). Bolna publishes no OpenAPI spec — **that premise is SUPERSEDED by D-350, which found the spec they do publish; the CONCLUSION below survives it, see D-187's note in `tests/poller_guarantee_test.py`** — so whether a listing row is as rich as `GET /executions/{execution_id}` is UNVERIFIED, and the conformance suite cannot fail on it either: `FakeEngine.list_executions` builds rows with the same `_snapshot_from` as its fetch, and the Bolna stub returned whole `BOLNA_COMPLETED` documents. Under the premise being wrong the failure is silent and total for one population — a completed call whose pipeline died, on an agent with no extraction schema and a tenant with no CRM endpoint, implies nothing, reads `settled` forever, and is never transcribed, metered or invoiced with no alert anywhere. The probe now confirms an EMPTY expectation set against the authenticated read before believing it, bounded by three conditions (`not expected` — the row carried neither cost nor transcript; `not any(present)` — the database holds nothing either, so a call whose pipeline ran is answered from its own artefacts with no vendor request; `late` — past `PIPELINE_STALL_AFTER`), which costs a genuinely silent call a handful of reads over its whole life rather than one per tick. A failing read PROPAGATES into `reconciliation_probe_incomplete`, which already reports repairs as a floor. **(2) `VoiceEngine.end_call` had no docstring, no stated semantics and no conformance clause, and the adapters disagreed underneath it**: `BolnaEngine` POSTs `/executions/{id}/stop` and `CartesiaEngine` POSTs `/agents/calls/{id}/end`, both surfacing the vendor's 404 as `engine_rejected`, while `FakeEngine` shrugged — so the offline pipeline (DEV-SETUP §3) reported a hang-up nobody performed. The contract now states the answer (RAISE — symmetric with `transfer`, deliberately not with `delete_agent`, because this method's caller is a control plane whose one observable failure is claiming to have stopped a call it did not), `FakeEngine` raises, and a clause pins it for all four subjects. Both vendor stubs' stop/end routes are now stateful for the reason their GET routes already are — a 200 for every id made the clause unfailable — and each carries a MARKED ASSUMPTION that the 404 is inferred, not captured (pilot gate 2). **(3) `_persist_transcript`'s upsert was partial**: `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET text, text_redacted` left `speaker`, `lang`, `start_ms`, `end_ms` at the first run's values and left the tail of a longer earlier reading in place, so a re-drive produced rows nobody spoke. Reachable through OUR parser, not only a fickle vendor: `bolna.parse_transcript` indexes by POSITION and drops a leading line it cannot attribute, so two fetches disagreeing about the opening line are off by one for the whole call and every turn inherits the other reading's speaker — and `speaker` drives the speaker-aware extractor (the reason `SAMPLE_TURNS` has the CALLER ask to book), the client's transcript view and the QA sample. The upsert now refreshes every column and deletes what this reading does not claim, matched on the indices written rather than on a length (contiguity is a property of today's parsers, not of `TranscriptTurn`). | **Each was a premise nothing could see.** (1) and (2) are the same defect class the conformance suite exists to catch, hiding in the two places the suite does not look: a method with no clause, and a field both adapters happen to fill. CLAUDE.md's rule is that an unverified vendor behaviour is a gate or a marked assumption, never a silent premise — the poller's richness assumption was a silent premise carrying D-31's entire guarantee of record, and `end_call`'s was one carrying the only observable failure a control-plane hang-up has. (3) is the "half-written row" class: an upsert that refreshes some columns of a row it is replacing is a fabrication that type-checks. **WHAT IT COSTS:** (1) adds at most one `get_execution` per bare completed call per tick past the grace window, for the ~3 ticks the 30-minute listing window admits it; the conditions are written so a healthy call never reaches the vendor at all. **WHAT CLOSES THE REMAINING UNKNOWNS, by name:** OPERATIONS §2 gate 6 records what a real Bolna listing row actually carries — if it is fetch-quality, (1) becomes belt-and-braces and stays; gate 2 records whether the vendor refuses a stop for an execution it is not running, which is what turns the stubs' marked assumption into a captured contract. Both need a Bolna account, which is the external blocker. |
| D-188 | **The production image had an empty virtualenv, the `.env` the deploy demands was one `Settings()` could not load, and the nginx floor was two releases below what the config needs — a first-deploy readiness audit, executed rather than read** | Five findings from walking the whole first-deploy path with the commands actually run, and their fixes. **(1) `Dockerfile` called `uv sync` without `--all-packages` in both phases.** The workspace root is `package = false` with `dependencies = []`, so uv resolved the root's empty list, installed nothing and exited 0: the shipped image's `site-packages` held THREE entries and not one third-party package. No service could start, `alembic upgrade head` could not run, and all three `scripts.*` modules `vps-deploy.sh` invokes through `compose run` would have died on their first import. Measured both ways: 3 entries before, 127 after. `--group errors` is added in the same line, because DEPLOYMENT §8's per-host `uv sync --all-packages --group errors` is an instruction the containerized architecture cannot obey (§2 puts no Python on the host; the venv is an image layer owned by a non-root user), so `sentry-sdk` was unreachable and `SENTRY_DSN` could never be more than a setting. The uv image is also pinned by digest, closing §4d item 1. **(2) `Settings` refused the prescribed `.env`.** `model_config` is `env_file='.env', extra='forbid'`, and pydantic-settings applies `forbid` to keys read from the DOTENV FILE — so the three object-store credentials that DEPLOYMENT §6 requires, that `vps-deploy.sh::preflight` ABORTS without, and that `check_deploy_env` validates, made `Settings()` raise three `extra_forbidden` errors for every process whose cwd is the deploy root. `calevate_shared.config` gains `SDK_OWNED_ENV_KEYS` and a `DotEnvSettingsSource` subclass that drops exactly those keys; `check_deploy_env.OBJECT_STORE_CREDENTIALS` aliases the constant and `check_env_parity.SDK_ENV_KEYS` asserts against it. `tests/deploy_env_file_loadable_test.py` is the regression, run red first. **(3) nginx.** `infra/nginx/` uses the standalone `http2 on;` directive, which appeared in nginx **1.25.1**; §2 said `nginx >= 1.24` and §1 says Ubuntu 22.04 (1.18) — on 1.24 `nginx -t` answers `unknown directive "http2"` and NO server block loads. §2 now says 1.25.1 with the reason, and `preflight_plan` refuses below `NGINX_MIN_VERSION` before anything is built. **(4) §2's "Python is NOT needed on the host" is false** for `scripts/backup/app-python.sh` — `notify.sh` defaults its sink to `alert-to-app.sh`, which exits 78 without the host venv, so every backup alarm reaches journald and nobody else — and for `scripts/bootstrap_admin.py`, whose documented `uv run` form cannot execute on the VPS at all. One gate in front of every tenant-realm read an operator can reach, including the recording D-181 moved onto `calls:read_raw`. The shape used instead is the one the industry converged on for assuming authority into another account's data: AWS STS `AssumeRole` takes the MFA code ONCE and returns a session credential with a bounded life, and a CHAINED role session is capped at one hour and cannot be extended past it (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_temp_request.html; repost.aws/knowledge-center/iam-role-chaining-limit). `auth_time` is the registered OIDC claim for exactly this question, so the ceiling is enforced with no `impersonation_grants` table — the module docstring's argument against one is untouched. Effective ceiling is 1 h + `GRANT_TTL`: capping `exp` at `auth_time + VIEW_AS_MAX_AGE` would make the boundary exact and the last grant arbitrarily short, which the console reads as "stale, re-mint" — a mint loop against an INSERT-ONLY ledger (hard rule 4). **REJECTED: reusing `X-Impersonation-Grant` for the renewal input.** That header means "this request is being made INSIDE the named tenant" and `core/auth.py` reads it beside `X-Impersonate-Org`; a mint is made from the operator's own admin session and is inside nothing. RFC 8693 carries the token being exchanged in the body for the same reason. **REJECTED: splitting the gate's two halves at this call site** so the echo is demanded on renewals too — `core/stepup.py` demands them together precisely so no route ends up with one, and a live grant for this tenant is stronger evidence of both intent and presence than an echo a stolen cookie satisfies trivially. **FAIL-CLOSED BY CONSTRUCTION**: `renewable_grant` is TOTAL — absent, forged, expired, another operator's, another tenant's and an unreadable `auth_time` all return `None`, and `None` sends the caller to the STRICTER path. No input can make it return a grant `verify_grant` would refuse. **THE SEAM THAT WAS ALREADY OPEN**: the console had NO step-up prompt at all, so the fifteen pre-existing gated routes were reachable only inside the five minutes after a sign-in and an operator's only remedy was to sign out and back in. That is fixed here for all sixteen, not just for this one. **NOT FIXED, NAMED**: the ops console's writes still render a `reauthentication_required` refusal rather than raising the prompt — the transport cannot retry those POSTs, because `client.ts`'s rule is that a repeated POST needs proof the refusal executed nothing, and only this route has that proof (`step_up.require` runs before `mint_grant` and before `write_audit`; `tests/impersonation_stepup_test.py` asserts the absent start row on every refusing branch). Wiring each of those call sites to prompt-then-retry is per-route work with a per-route safety argument, not a transport rung. |
| D-211 | **BACKEND-PATTERNS §7 said raw-transcript access is a step-up action while the client realm has no second factor — the conflict is resolved by realm, not by deleting the sentence** | §7's list now reads "high-risk **admin-realm** actions" and the raw-transcript item splits in two, each true of the realm it names: on the CLIENT realm an owner reading their own transcript is `calls:read_raw` + a `transcript.read_raw` audit row in the same transaction, by design; on the ADMIN realm it is step-up, taken at the impersonation door (D-210). SECURITY-COMPLIANCE §5 gains both bullets. §7's heading and opening paragraph stop saying "Clerk owns sessions" (D-177 deleted the vendor), and the two other dangling vendor references in that document — the load-shed paragraph's `/v1/auth` aside and the ops-config bullet — are corrected to what is true. | **WHY THE DOC WAS THE WRONG HALF, AND ONLY HALF-WRONG.** `MFA_REQUIRED_REALMS` is `{"admin"}` (D-170 removed TOTP, enrolment and recovery codes), so `StepUp.present` is False for every client caller: declaring the gate on `/v1/calls/{id}/transcript/raw` would not tighten the route, it would DELETE it — a tenant owner reading their own call refused with a remediation pointing at `/v1/auth/admin/step-up`, an endpoint their realm does not have. **WHY ROLE + AUDIT IS THE RIGHT CONTROL THERE**, rather than a gap to be closed later: the threat models are not the same shape. On the admin realm the reader is an outsider to the data — our staff reading a customer's customers' conversations — and step-up defends the tenant against us and against a stolen operator credential. On the client realm the reader is the Data Fiduciary's own `owner` reading recordings of their own callers; that is the controller exercising controllership, and the control that matters is the one that makes it attributable, which is the audit row hard rule 5 already requires and `staff` never holding `calls:read_raw` (D-181 put the AUDIO on the same pair). **WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER**: a client-realm second factor existing at all. That is a product decision about Indian SMB owners and email deliverability which D-170 already took, and reversing it is its own decision-log entry — not a consequence of this one, and not an engineering gap being deferred. **WHY THE SENTENCE WAS AMENDED RATHER THAN DELETED**: it was never wrong about the admin realm, and D-210 makes it true there for the first time; deleting it would have thrown away a correct requirement to resolve an ambiguity about which realm it addressed. |

| D-216 | **The facet rail's ceiling is derived from its own budget, and D-209's LIMIT stops spilling 13 MB to disk** | `crm.service` gains `FACET_RAIL_BUDGET_MS = 200` and `FACET_QUERY_COST_MS = 50` (measured), and `MAX_FACET_FIELDS` becomes `FACET_RAIL_BUDGET_MS // FACET_QUERY_COST_MS` — four, from eight. `lead_facets`' aggregate moves into a `WITH counted AS MATERIALIZED (…)` with the declared-first `ORDER BY` and the `LIMIT` outside it. | D-322 | **Two deadlines were written by the application's clock and judged by the database's** | `idempotency_records.expires_at` and `invitations.expires_at` are now written as `now() + make_interval(secs => :ttl_s)`, the same clock every reader compares them with. `tests/reliability_late_report_test.py::test_the_idempotency_ttl_is_measured_by_one_clock` and `tests/admin_security_test.py::test_the_invitation_deadline_is_measured_by_one_clock` age the transaction with a `pg_sleep` and assert `expires_at - created_at` is EXACTLY the TTL. | **WHY.** Both columns were `datetime.now(UTC) + TTL` while both readers use the database clock — `sweep_idempotency`'s `expires_at < now()`, and `expires_at > now()` in the pending-invitation probe and in `accept_invitation`'s burn. That is wrong twice. By the host skew, which is unbounded and invisible. And, on every deployment regardless of skew, by the AGE OF THE TRANSACTION: Postgres `now()` is transaction START time while the Python expression is evaluated when the statement is built, so a row minted after other work in the same transaction quietly outlives its stated TTL by however long that work took — measured at **+501ms on a 24h key and +506ms on a 72h invitation** with a single 500ms statement ahead of it, and `create_invitation` really does run after three reads. The repo already made this correction once, for the outbox's retry rung (`_BACKOFF_INTERVAL_SQL`); these are the two places it had not reached. Every other deadline in the tree was checked and is self-consistent: the whole of `authn` writes and compares with the app clock (`now=` is injectable for testability), and `consent`/`preference_scrub` do the same. |

| D-350 | **Bolna publishes an OpenAPI specification, and this repository asserted the opposite in thirty-one places** | The vendor's own GitHub organisation carries it: `bolna-ai/skills`, `references/openapi.yml`, OpenAPI 3.1.0, 5977 lines, described in its sibling `references/bolna-core.md` as a "mirror of https://www.bolna.ai/docs/api-reference/openapi.yml" with the instruction *"Treat the YAML as the canonical schema if a SKILL.md and the spec disagree."* Pinned at `28b24aa504389ec69584301ea32545946e256409`, `md5 5597f7da080d47564696bc05c12e9112`. `docs/vendor/bolna/hosted-oas.md` is new and holds the pin, the re-fetch command, the complete endpoint inventory and the facts it settles. The evidence taxonomy gains **VERIFIED-OAS** (the spec) and **VERIFIED-VENDOR-REPO** (the SKILL.md/`references/` prose) above `VERIFIED-OSS`, and retires **REPORTED-DOCS**. Four defects follow from it and are logged separately: D-351, D-353, D-354, D-355. One claim it settles in our FAVOUR: `13.203.39.153` is confirmed as the single webhook source address, matching `DEFAULT_BOLNA_SOURCE_IPS` exactly. **One claim it does NOT settle, against a first reading of this row that said it did: the cost UNIT.** The OAS says "in cents" verbatim on `total_cost` and all five `cost_breakdown` members — but `references/execution-payload.md`, the same repo at the same commit, calls `total_cost` "Bolna cost in account currency", which is major units. The vendor contradicts itself on the one field the money path divides by. `_ASSUMED_MINOR_UNITS_PER_MAJOR = 100` is unchanged, because `bolna-core.md` publishes the tiebreak ("treat the YAML as the canonical schema if a SKILL.md and the spec disagree") and it points at cents — but a precedence rule reconciling two documents is not an observation of a server, so it stays a MARKED ASSUMPTION under hard rule 7 and OPERATIONS §2 gate 7 now scores the unit as well as the currency. The reconciling reading ("minor units OF the account currency") is coherent and is probably true; it is written down as a hypothesis because neither document says it. | **HOW A FALSE PREMISE SURVIVED THIRTY-ONE RESTATEMENTS.** `docs.bolna.ai`, `www.bolna.ai`, `docs.bolna.dev` and `api.bolna.ai` are genuinely blocked by this environment's egress proxy — re-measured, still true, and correctly recorded as "no hosted documentation page in this repository has been read by anyone here". What happened next is the defect: a statement about a blocked HOST was allowed to become a statement about an absent DOCUMENT, and then to become the stated justification for a truncation heuristic, a guessed request body, a hand-maintained status list, a marked assumption on the money path, and several pilot gates whose only job was to learn a published fact. `github.com` and `raw.githubusercontent.com` were reachable the entire time — `docs/vendor/bolna/oss-harvest.md` is a full clone read at source, which proves it. One GitHub code search for `"api.bolna.ai/v2/agent"` surfaced the vendor's repo in seconds. **The generalisable rule, now in `docs/vendor/bolna/README.md`: before filing a vendor fact as UNVERIFIED, ask whether the vendor publishes it somewhere reachable — their GitHub org, their SDKs, PyPI, npm — not whether their docs site answered.** The old README listed exactly three evidence classes and none of them was "the vendor's own machine-readable contract", so there was no slot to file one in even if someone had found it. |

The call is alive and the vendor is holding it; we told the client it was dead, and the campaign's failure rate counted a success as a loss. **AND THE SAME ENUM ANSWERS D-260's OPEN QUESTION**: there is no `voicemail` STATUS, so `CallStatus.voicemail` is unreachable from this engine and voicemail arrives as the boolean `answered_by_voice_mail` on an execution whose status is plain `completed`. | D-352 | **"Bolna webhooks are at-most-once with no retry" was a load-bearing claim about a program that is not the hosted deliverer** | Documentation and comments only — the design was already right. The adapter's module docstring, `calevate_shared/config`'s note and `apps/workers/pipeline.py`'s poller block are corrected. | **WHERE THE FALSE CLAIM CAME FROM, AND WHY IT MATTERED EVEN THOUGH NOTHING CHANGED.** It was VERIFIED-OSS: `bolna-ai/bolna`'s delivery code really is a single `aiohttp` POST with no retry and swallowed errors. That is the SELF-HOSTED framework, not the hosted deliverer, and the two differ. The claim was labelled with the strongest class this repo had, sat at the top of the adapter as one of three "load-bearing" properties, and was cited in the poller's own docstring as why the poller exists. It is the cleanest available illustration of why `VERIFIED-OSS` now ranks BELOW the two first-party hosted classes rather than beside them: it was not wrong about the code it read, it was wrong about which program runs in production. The poller's justification is unchanged — a receiver that is DOWN gets no delivery to retry — but it now rests on a true sentence. |
| D-353 | **The guarantee of record called an endpoint that does not exist, and so did the campaign halt** | Two wrong routes, both corrected with tests that fail without the fix. **(1)** `list_executions` issued `GET /executions?created_after=<iso>`; the spec has no `/executions` collection at all — its only `/executions/...` entries are `GET /executions/{execution_id}` and `.../log` — and no `created_after` parameter anywhere. The listing is PER AGENT: `GET /v2/agent/{agent_id}/executions`, filtered by `from`/`to` on `created_at`, paginated by `page_number`/`page_size` (max 50) with a `has_more` flag, envelope `{page_number, page_size, total, has_more, data[]}`. The adapter now discovers agents through `GET /v2/agent/all` and walks each one's pages, which is the same fan-out shape `CartesiaEngine.list_executions` already has for the same reason. `_LISTING_PAGE_SIZES`, `_claims_more` and `_next_link` are DELETED, not repaired. **(2)** `end_call` issued `POST /executions/{id}/stop`; the route is `POST /call/{execution_id}/stop`. `tests/bolna_listing_test.py` is rewritten around the real endpoint and `tests/bolna_contract_test.py` is new; the conformance stub's routes are corrected too. | **WHAT EACH WOULD HAVE COST ON THE FIRST LIVE TICK.** The listing: `vendor_request` turns a 404 into a raised dependency error, `reconcile_executions` catches it and alerts `reconciliation_fetch_failed`, and ten minutes later it does it again — forever, with the console showing an engine fault rather than a wrong URL, and D-31's guarantee of record never running once. The stop: a 404 on the one call the campaign path makes to pull a queued dial back after a DNC addition or the big red switch, i.e. a lead that gets called after asking not to be. **WHY NO TEST CAUGHT EITHER.** The conformance stub answered both invented routes, because it was written from the same guess as the adapter — a stub built from the adapter's assumptions agrees with it forever, which is why `tests/bolna_contract_test.py` asserts URLs and body KEYS against the spec rather than round-tripping through a fixture. **THE HEURISTIC WAS NOT A MISTAKE UNDER ITS PREMISE AND IS SIMPLY WRONG UNDER THE TRUE ONE**: `_LISTING_PAGE_SIZES` inferred truncation from a row count landing on a conventional page size, which under the real contract fires on every healthy tick that returns 20 or 50 rows. |

The second is silent accounting: `resolve_campaign_contact` matches on `last_call_id` AND `status = 'dialing'`, so once the reaper moved the row the call that actually connected could never be recorded — the campaign's reached count under-reported it and the contact could still be exhausted into `failed` having been reached. | D-368 ⚠CLOSED by migration b2e6f10c94d7 (by a FOURTH route this row never contemplated, and the RECOMMENDED option (1) was deliberately NOT taken — see the closing paragraph) | **A knowledge source is the one expirable artefact a tenant can hold without ever publishing an agent, so the nightly retention sweep cannot reach it** | `retention._due_tenants` derives the worklist from `SELECT DISTINCT tenant_id FROM engine_agent_routes` — the global bridge, so the sweep needs no admin role and no RLS exemption (hard rule 1). D-179 then added `kb` as a sixth retention category, and `kb/service.reject_source` moves a source `pending_approval → rejected` with no engine involvement: a tenant that uploads a document, has it refused, and never publishes an agent holds a `kb_sources` row that `_KB_EXPIRABLE` matches, a `kb_documents` row holding whatever they uploaded, and a `retention_policies` row promising 365 days — and is in no worklist. **CLOSED by migration `b2e6f10c94d7`**: a new global table `retention_worklist` (tenant_id, a reason from a closed one-value CHECK, a timestamp), maintained by an AFTER INSERT trigger on `kb_sources` and BACKFILLED in the same transaction, with `_due_tenants` now reading `SELECT tenant_id FROM engine_agent_routes UNION SELECT tenant_id FROM retention_worklist ORDER BY tenant_id`. The model is `compliance/models.RetentionWorklistEntry`, the table is an ordinary `db/registry.TENANT_TABLES` entry, and the tests are `tests/retention_worklist_test.py` (eleven, sabotage-verified, including the cross-tenant zero-rows check hard rule 1 requires). Both docstrings that asserted the invariant carry the reproduction and now record the closure. | **MEASURED, and the measurement is what makes it small and precise.** A fresh organization has all six policies and zero routes; `sweep_tenant()` called DIRECTLY on such a tenant returns `{'kb_versions': 1}` and removes the source and its chunks. So the sweep ARM is correct and only the WORKLIST is short — which is why no sweep logic changed. The population is bounded to `rejected`: `archived` is only ever produced by `_detach_superseded`, i.e. by a publish, which mints the route. **WHY IT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN A FIX.** Both closures are tenancy changes, not sweep changes. (1) Read `kb_sources.tenant_id` cross-tenant — a THIRD entry in `db/registry.RLS_EXEMPT_TENANT_COLUMNS`, on a table holding CLIENT CONTENT, where the two existing entries hold routing keys and a hash chain; the registry says a third "costs a visible argument" precisely so this is not done in passing. (2) Walk `organizations` under `admin_session`, the shape `qa_sampling.draw_qa_samples` already uses — correct and simple, and it reinstates the per-tenant fan-out D-57 and P6.2 deliberately removed from this job (measured then at ~16k sessions / ~3 minutes). (3) Delete a rejected source at rejection time — cheapest, and it changes product behaviour: the rejection reason is what an operator reads, and zero is not the client's 365-day policy. **RECOMMENDED: (1)**, scoped to `SELECT DISTINCT tenant_id` and nothing else, because it costs one statement per night against an index that already exists (`ix_kb_sources_superseded`) and leaves the sweep's per-tenant cost shape untouched — but it widens a read on client content and that is the founder's call, not an audit's. **(1) WAS RECOMMENDED AND WAS NOT TAKEN, and that is worth more here than the closure itself.** A FOURTH route none of the three above contemplated stores the FACT rather than deriving it: `retention_worklist` holds one row per (tenant, reason) — a tenant id, a reason from a closed one-value CHECK, and a timestamp — so `kb_sources` keeps its FORCEd policy untouched and `RLS_EXEMPT_TENANT_COLUMNS` gains NOTHING AT ALL. Reading one derived fact is not worth a global read of the client content it is derived from, and the registry's "a third entry costs a visible argument" reads better as a price to refuse than as one to pay carefully. It also answers this row's own objection to a presence table — "a second bridge to keep in step with the first" — because a DATABASE TRIGGER maintains it rather than a service function: the sentence *a tenant that holds a knowledge source is in the retention worklist* then holds for every writer of that table, including ones nobody has written yet and an operator inserting by hand mid-incident. That is how hard rule 4's ledgers are already enforced, and it is the right mechanism for an obligation that is legal rather than operational. The trigger is deliberately NOT conditioned on `status`: registering a tenant with nothing expired costs one cheap probe a night and missing one costs a DPDP obligation, so the failure directions are not symmetric and the sentence has no status in it. **THE MIGRATION IS WHAT CLOSED IT, NOT THE CODE**, because enforcement only reaches forward — the backfill runs as the owner role in the same transaction as the trigger and registers every tenant already in the hole. **MEASURED AT THE MOMENT OF CLOSURE, on the development database: 353 tenants held knowledge sources and had no `engine_agent_routes` row** — that many were outside every retention sweep this platform has ever run, which is the number this row was missing when it called the population "bounded". The RLS shape ended up NARROWER than the neighbour it was modelled on: `tenant_isolation` is the strict own-tenant form for every verb, and a second `FOR SELECT USING (GUC IS NULL)` policy widens reads to sessions carrying no tenant — the retention worker and nothing else — where `engine_agent_routes`' `FOR SELECT USING (true)` is readable cross-tenant from a CLIENT session too, and where nothing untenanted may write here at all. | D-432 | **THE BIG RED SWITCH GREW ITS SECOND ARM: a halt now recalls the dials the vendor is already holding, and `end_call` has a caller. Counted as unstoppable either way, which over-reports the phones that will ring rather than under-reporting them — the safe direction — and the gate is four real calls on an account nobody has yet. | **The gap was live, not theoretical, and it was invisible in exactly the way D-428 predicted.** `POST /call` answers `status: queued` for every dial (`bolna-findings/mirror/pages/api-reference/calls/make.md:25`) and surplus over the account's concurrency ceiling is QUEUED rather than rejected (`.../pricing/outbound-calling-concurrency.md:41`) in a queue we cannot see, cancel or DNC-scrub; on a trial account that ceiling is 2 (`:15`) against an outbound pool of 6. So an operator halting at 20:55 IST was told dialling stopped while the vendor went on ringing phones past 21:00, with our records showing every contact lawfully cleared by `check_dispatch`. **`recall_requested_at` is the part a reviewer would call unnecessary, and it is the part that keeps the alarm honest.** Without it a second halt — or an arq retry — re-POSTs a stop for every dial already stopped, takes the vendor's refusal for an already-stopped execution, and raises "could not stop N dials" on work that succeeded. A false alarm on the one control an operator reads literally mid-incident is worse than no alarm; the stamp makes a re-run see only what the last run did not reach, which is also what lets a capped run be finished by re-posting the halt. The job re-reads the halt before stopping anything, so an operator who released inside the queue latency does not have their campaign torn down. **ENQUEUED DIRECTLY RATHER THAN THROUGH THE OUTBOX**, which is this repo's default and is the wrong tool here: `set_platform_status` commits the halt on its own connection before the handler reaches this line, so there is no shared fate left for the outbox to preserve, and its 10-second dispatch tick would be ten seconds of ringing bought for nothing. A failed enqueue ALARMS (`dial_recall_not_queued`) and does not refuse the request — telling an operator the switch did not throw when it did sends them to throw it again. **WHAT STAYS OPEN AND WHY IT IS NOT THIS ROW**: D-428(b), the DNC half. `end_call` cannot stop a call in progress, so a cancel that races an answer must not be recorded as a prevented call, and that is a compliance-record decision rather than a wiring one. | D-433 | **FIVE GUARDRAILS COULD NOT RUN ON THE MACHINE THIS REPOSITORY IS DEVELOPED ON, AND THREE OF THEM FAILED BY LAPSING THEIR OWN EXEMPTIONS RATHER THAN BY CRASHING** | Two portability defects, one class each, found by running `make guardrails` locally before a push. **(1) Encoding.** Forty-three files — ten guardrail scripts and thirty-three test modules — read the tree with a bare `Path.read_text()`, which decodes with the platform default (cp1252 here) and dies on the first non-ASCII byte in a tree written entirely in UTF-8. `check_wiring`, `check_alarm_wiring`, `check_job_wiring` and `check_half_wired` aborted with a `UnicodeDecodeError` before checking anything, and pytest could not even COLLECT: `tests/auth_email_delivery_test.py` reads a source file at import time, so the whole suite — and therefore `make coverage-ratchet`, hard rule 10's gate — died at collection. Every read is now `encoding="utf-8"`. **(2) Path separators.** `check_ledger_immutability`, `check_alarm_wiring`, `check_job_wiring` and `check_half_wired` compare `str(Path)` against exemption registries written with `/`, so on Windows no exemption ever matched: the ledger gate reported `platform_secrets` mutations that are the recorded D-97 KEK re-wrap, the job gate reported the outbox dispatcher's dynamic enqueue, and the half-wired gate flagged a `TODO` inside its own explanation of what a `TODO` marker is. All four now compare `.as_posix()`. **(3)** `check_deploy_workflow` piped each workflow `run:` block to `bash -n` with `text=True`, which on Windows translates every `\r\n` to `\n` on the way down the pipe; bash read the carriage return as part of the last token and reported the production deploy script as a syntax error. It now pipes bytes. | **A gate that cannot run where the work happens is a gate that only CI enforces, and CI runs after the push.** That alone would be worth fixing. What makes it a decision-log row is the SHAPE of the second defect: those three gates did not crash, they FAILED — with plausible, specific, entirely false findings, on files the author had not touched. New `core/rbac.SUPERADMIN_ONLY_PERMISSIONS` names the four, and `tests/admin_operators_test.py` asserts `SUPERADMIN_PERMISSIONS - ROLE_PERMISSIONS["operator"] == SUPERADMIN_ONLY_PERMISSIONS` — an equation over the CONSTANTS, not a hand-typed list, so a permission added to the `Permission` type cannot land on a side nobody chose. **THE SIDEBAR HALF SHIPPED TOO**: the three config/credential panels moved off `/admin/ops` onto their own screen at `/admin/ops/config` (a nav entry needs a destination, and one screen carrying three permissions could only declare one of them in the nav), with a `Platform configuration` entry gated on `platform:config` — the ONE entry in either shell that is ABSENT rather than shown-and-dead for a session that may not use it, argued at `apps/web/src/app/admin/layout.tsx::renderItem`. | **THE DEFECT THIS FOUND WAS NOT THE FEATURE, AND IT WAS LIVE.** `ROLE_PERMISSIONS` is ONE flat dict over BOTH realms, so a client `owner` genuinely holds `org:manage`, `agents:write` and `kb:write` — strings that around a dozen `/v1/admin/**` routes declare. A console route that omitted `realm="admin"` therefore satisfied every clause the registry had and was reachable by every tenant owner on the platform. `ADMIN_REALM_PREFIXES` + `route_realms()`, asserted at BOOT rather than in a test, closes it: on the console's own paths **the realm is what keeps clients out, not the permission**. The live table was already clean, which is the point — the assertion is what stops the next route being the one that is not. **NO SELF-GRANTING IS THREE INDEPENDENT FACTS RATHER THAN ONE CHECK**: the surface sits behind the very role it edits; `_refuse_self` refuses a role change or a revocation aimed at the actor, in both tiers; and authority is re-read from `admin_users` on every request, so a demotion or a revocation binds the session already in flight. **THE "THERE IS ALWAYS A LIVE SUPERADMIN" INVARIANT IS A CONSEQUENCE OF THOSE THREE, AND DELIBERATELY HAS NO `count(*)` GUARD** — the branch could never fire, and an unreachable defensive arm is precisely what hard rule 10 fails the ratchet over; `tests/admin_operators_test.py` proves the invariant by driving the flow instead. **AND "THERE WILL ONLY BE ONE SUPER ADMIN" IS DELIBERATELY NOT CAPPED EITHER [23 Aug 2026], FOR A DIFFERENT REASON — THERE IS NO BREAK-GLASS.** The founder's sentence is a fact about who they intend to appoint, and turning it into an `AT MOST one` guard was considered and refused after establishing that nothing in this repository can mint or restore a superadmin outside the app: `bootstrap_first_admin` REFUSES the moment any live operator holds a password (state 3, no `--force`) — which is exactly the state a lockout occurs in — `scripts/seed_dev.py::_upsert_admin` is gated on `APP_ENV=local` and only ever INSERTs, and `authn/operators.set_operator_role` is the only statement in the tree that updates `admin_users.role`, sitting behind the very role it would restore. With a cap in force `_refuse_self` also makes the role NON-TRANSFERABLE: promoting a successor is refused while the incumbent exists and the incumbent cannot demote themselves, so no order of operations hands the platform to another person, and the one in-app recovery that exists today — appointing a standby superadmin before you need one — would be deleted. What holds the count at one instead is the narrow default role, `admin:operators`, a step-up bound to the ROLE and a ledger row; the residual risk (lose that one account and there is no in-product way back) is stated in `apps/api/authn/operators.py` and in SEC-COMP §5 rather than legislated away. If a cap is ever wanted, a documented break-glass has to land FIRST. **IMPERSONATION WIDENS THE TIER BY NOTHING**: `requires()` already refuses any `MUTATING_PERMISSIONS` member while impersonating regardless of role, and `admin:operators` is in that set — so the most privileged session this product can issue still cannot hand out an admin account from inside a client dashboard. **STEP-UP IS BOUND TO THE ROLE, NOT THE ADDRESS** (`add_operator:<role>`), because an email address in a step-up token reaches access logs and hard rule 6's argument does not stop at phone numbers. **WHAT THE 23 AUG CORRECTION COSTS, NAMED RATHER THAN IMPLIED.** `calls:read_raw` is not in `MUTATING_PERMISSIONS`, so moving it into the normal tier opens six client-realm routes to a normal admin inside a D-22 view-as session that were previously refused outright: the unredacted transcript, the recording, both shapes of the unmasked CSV export, the DPDP subject-access export and a delivered webhook payload. Every one of them writes its own `audit_log` row, and entry to the session needed a second factor at the impersonation door (D-210) — so the control changes from "they cannot" to "they can, attributably", which is the same control a tenant `owner` reading their own data is under. `tests/impersonation_audit_test.py` used to assert the 403 and now asserts the ledger row, inverted in place rather than deleted. `leads:dispatch` costs nothing reachable today: it IS in `MUTATING_PERMISSIONS`, D-22 refuses it to an impersonating admin, `current_any` resolves the admin realm only when the impersonation header is present, and every route declaring it is client-realm — the grant puts the boundary where the founder drew it so a future admin-realm dispatch surface does not re-litigate it. **TWO SUPERADMIN-ONLY ACTS RIDE ON `ops:manage` RATHER THAN DECLARING IT**, and both survive unchanged because `ops:manage` is one of the four: tenant erasure (`compliance/tenant_erasure_routes.py` checks `role_has(role, "ops:manage")`) and raising or removing a client's spend ceiling (`admin/routes.py::record_commercial_terms`). **SECRETS: A NON-SUPER ADMIN GETS NOTHING, NOT EVEN THE MASKED INVENTORY.** Write is settled by PLATFORM-CONFIG §10, whose risk acceptance rests verbatim on that permission being held by fewer people than `admin:tenants`. READ is refused on a separate ground: `GET /v1/ops/secrets` is an INVENTORY of which vendor credentials exist and which are missing, which is a targeting oracle — the same argument D-128 made for `/healthz/ready`. **THE AMBIGUITY THIS ROW FLAGGED IS CLOSED AND THE NARROW READING WAS RIGHT.** "Admins who are not super admins and do have access to some things like the ops config panel where I put in all the API keys" read, on one parse, as granting operators that panel; the docs won per CLAUDE.md and the conflict was recorded in `apps/api/ops/secret_routes.py` rather than decided silently. Asked directly, the founder settled it the same way — "only super admin has access to ops config panel" — so the one-line widening that paragraph held open is WITHDRAWN, not still pending. **NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY**: no `alert()` on operator creation (it would owe a `runbooks/alarm-index.md` row; the hash-chained audit ledger plus superadmin-only plus step-up is the control), and no `costly` rate-limit profile on the two mail-sending routes, which inherit `admin_api` and are already superadmin-only behind step-up. |
| D-458 | **WHAT A MONTH COSTS IS A FIELD ON THE ENDPOINT, NOT A SUM IN THE BROWSER — AND IT IS THE SAME EXPRESSION THE MARGIN PANEL BOOKS AS REVENUE.** | `UsagePanelOut` published three charge components — `monthly_fee_inr`, `overage_cost_inr` and, since D-455, `llm_surcharge_inr` — and no total, so the two client screens that print "this month so far" (the usage page and the dashboard's money tile) had to add rupees in JavaScript. `apps/web/src/lib/money.ts` did it correctly, in whole paise, and its own docstring said the better shape was a field on the endpoint and that it could not add one. `billing/service.py::month_charges_inr` is that field's arithmetic: the retainer plus `calling_revenue_inr`, returned UNQUANTIZED so its two callers round once each — `usage_summary` publishes `to_paise(...)` as `month_charges_inr`, and `margin_for_tenant` subtracts a cost and divides before anything is rounded. `money.ts` and `money.test.tsx` are DELETED rather than left beside it, `addRupees` with them (it had no other caller), and both screens read the field. **THERE IS NOW NO MONEY ADDITION ANYWHERE IN THE BROWSER**; `lib/llmRates.ts` still COMPARES two server-sent rates at their own scale, and says at its head that it is deliberately not where the deleted arithmetic returns to. | **THE TWO NUMBERS WERE ALREADY ONE NUMBER AND WERE COMPUTED TWICE.** What a client owes for a period and what we book as revenue for it are the same figure seen from two sides; `margin_for_tenant` summed its own `monthly_fee + calling_revenue_inr(...)` while the panel summed a different expression in a different language. That is exactly how a panel and a margin report come to disagree about a month, and D-455 exists because the same class of split had already happened one level down. One expression, two callers, and `tests/llm_model_surcharge_test.py` asserts the identity directly so re-inlining it fails. **WHY A BROWSER SUM IS NOT MERELY UNTIDY.** A rupee is an exact decimal STRING from the database to the pixel (hard rule 7's frontend shadow), and JavaScript has one numeric type: `Number("10159.00")` is how ₹10,159.00 reaches a screen as ₹10,158.999999999998 — on the screen a client checks against their own books. The deleted helper avoided that by converting to whole paise, which was right; the objection that stands is the other one — a total computed in the client is a second implementation of a bill, and the first thing to disagree with the invoice. **THE COMPONENTS STAY PUBLISHED, AND THAT IS NOT REDUNDANCY.** A client checking a statement needs to see the parts add up; what they must not need is for two of our own surfaces to agree by coincidence. **`month_charges_inr` IS NOT `spend_used_inr`, and the distinction is stated in both models because the names invite the confusion.** `spend_used_inr` is what has been METERED — the live counter on an open month, the ledger on a closed one — so on an open month it carries no retainer at all and answers "what have my calls drawn down". This answers "what will this month cost me". **THE DEFECT HISTORY IS WHY THE TEST CASES ARE THE SHAPE THEY ARE**: the dashboard tile printed `overage_cost_inr` alone under the word "spend", so it omitted the retainer, and after D-455 it also omitted an upgrade the client pays on every minute of their own choosing — an account INSIDE its allowance on the dearer model read ₹0.00 on its home screen and was invoiced an "AI model upgrade" line for the same month. That case is parametrized on both sides of the wire. **REJECTED — deriving the total in the fixtures too**: a test that recomputed the sum would re-implement the arithmetic the screens just stopped doing, and would agree with a broken screen. The fixtures state the figure. |
| D-459 | **ALL THREE LEGS GO ON OFFER: THE CLIENT BRINGS NO KEY, THE FOUNDER INSTALLS EVERY KEY, AND A PRICE NOBODY HERE CAN FETCH BECOMES AN OPERATOR ATTESTATION RATHER THAN A BLOCKED MODEL.** | D-456 built the three-leg catalogue but shipped with only Azure's two models selectable, because `LlmModelSpec.__post_init__` refused `selectable=True` on a price whose evidence was not `verified` — and no OpenAI or Google price is fetchable from this environment or from CI (every vendor pricing host is egress-blocked, re-measured 23 Aug 2026). The founder's directive removes the BYOK framing entirely: clients choose from models WE provide, the founder holds all three vendor accounts and installs all three keys in the ops console, so the product must offer the choices. **`SELECTABLE_LLM_MODELS` NO LONGER EQUALS `AZURE_OPENAI_MODELS`** — it is `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4.1-mini` (Azure), `gpt-5.4-mini` (OpenAI direct) and `gemini-2.5-flash` / `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` (Google): five models across three legs. **The price became an OPERATOR ATTESTATION.** A new `platform_model_prices` append-only ledger (migration `c7f1a9e34b62`, 9th hard-rule-4 table) holds the founder's attested INR-or-USD figure per model, entered in the ops Model Pricing panel; `billing/rates.py` reads the ATTESTED figure for `unit_cost_paid`, and `LlmModelSpec.price` narrows to a CATALOGUE REFERENCE (the vendor-published pre-fill, never billing). So hard rule 7 is satisfied structurally — the number that reaches money is one a human read off their own vendor console, not a search summary — and a model is OFFERABLE only when it is selectable AND its provider's credential is installed AND its price is attested (`agents/llm_models.offerable_models()`), which is why widening the selectable set ships no unpriced spend. | **WHAT IS OFFERED, AND WHY NOT THE REST — the constraint is cost per minute of call, not model prestige.** `gpt-5.4-mini` is the OpenAI budget model whose `reasoning_effort` defaults to `none` (vendor-confirmed, developers.openai.com), so no reasoning eats the 150-token voice budget; `gpt-5.4` and the 5.5/5.6 flagships are out of the per-minute budget and stay `selectable=False`. On Google, ONLY `gemini-2.5-flash` and `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` are offered: the engine can zero their thinking budget (`thinkingBudget=0`, vendor-confirmed), so they cannot go silent mid-call. **EVERY `gemini-3.x` IS REFUSED ON CORRECTNESS**, not cost or residency — Google's own docs (ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/generate-content/thinking) say Gemini 3 Flash/Flash-Lite "do not support full thinking-off" and `minimal` "does not guarantee that thinking is off", so a candidate can return with empty text at `finishReason: MAX_TOKENS` and the engine yields nothing ("Dead turn detected") — dead air on a phone line, no retry. `gemini-2.5-pro` is withheld as a cost tier. **THE GPT-5 TRAPS ARE NOW APPLIED AT THE WIRE**, not merely declared: `engine/bolna.py` reads `LlmModelSpec.traps` and sends `temperature: 1` and `max_completion_tokens` for a GPT-5 model (it sent `temperature: 0.1` unconditionally before, which a GPT-5 model rejects at CREATE). **THE SURCHARGE FLOORS AT ZERO** (D-455): a budget model cheaper than the base — `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` at a vendor-published $0.10/1M input undercuts `gpt-4o-mini`'s $0.165 Regional — carries NO surcharge and never a negative; `surchargeable_models_are_dearer` was the predicate that would have surcharged a client for saving us money. **THE RETIREMENT DATES WERE RE-VERIFIED (hard rule 11):** the `retires_on=2026-10-16` a past session wrote for GA `gemini-2.5-flash`/`-flash-lite` was WRONG — it was a dated PREVIEW-snapshot date conflated with the GA id; Google's own deprecations page (2026-08-13) announces no shutdown for either GA model, and OpenAI `gpt-5.4-mini` is active with no announced retirement (≥6-month-notice policy, none posted). Both corrected to no-announced-retirement, verified. **ADMINS CHANGE A CLIENT'S MODEL through the named-tenant admin route** `PUT /v1/admin/organizations/{org_id}/llm-defaults` (`admin:tenants`, audit-logged against the client's account), NOT by writing through a view-as session — D-22's read-only impersonation invariant is intact, and the write carries the admin's own identity, which is the stronger audit trail. **OPS CONFIG STAYS SUPER-ADMIN-ONLY (D-457):** the panel where these keys and prices are installed is one of the four super-admin-only surfaces. ⚠ **STILL OWED TO A HUMAN, NAMED:** the founder attests each new model's price in the ops console before it is offerable (that is the design, not a gap); and a per-AGENT admin override under impersonation is deliberately absent (the org-default admin route covers the account-level need; per-agent tuning stays the client's, or the founder confirms weakening D-22). |
| D-460 | **THE PER-AGENT EXTRACTION VARIABLES BECOME SELF-SERVE FOR CLIENTS AND ADMINS ALIKE, AND THE FIELD HINT IS RENAMED FOR WHAT IT IS.** (24 Aug 2026, supersedes D-21's admin-only clause) | The extraction schema (the variables the AI captures after a call) is now fully add/edit/delete-able by the CLIENT (owner role, self-serve) AND by Calevate admins/superadmin — no more "request changes through us". Both realms mirror the dual client+admin router pattern (client `org:manage` on their own agents; admin `admin:tenants` on any tenant via the named-tenant route, never a view-as write, so D-22 stays intact). One write path: a whole-list PUT validated by the existing `ExtractionSchemaSpec` (unique keys, enum needs values, no collision with the fixed Leads columns), idempotent (an identical list makes no new version). Each save is LIVE — it inserts a new `extraction_schemas` version and points the agent at it in one transaction, and the next call uses it; there is no draft/publish or test-run gate (the D-21 "test run before it goes live" UI copy is removed). Old versions stay, so historical Leads keep rendering by the version active at extraction time. The per-field free-text hint is renamed `description` → `reason` ("why this variable is needed"): it is the ONE optional AI hint per field, fed to the extraction prompt, and when empty the field name/label alone is used — exactly the prior behaviour, renamed for clarity, with a reversible JSONB data migration. | **THE MANAGED-SERVICE MOAT WAS NEVER THE SCHEMA GATE.** D-21 kept schema edits in-house because they "regenerate prompt hints and need a regression run" — but the generated prompt already degrades gracefully on an empty hint and validation already rejects a bad field, so gatekeeping bought friction, not safety; the moat is quality, compliance and the fixed status enum, none of which this touches. **`reason` REUSES THE EXISTING FIELD, IT DOES NOT ADD ONE** — the model already carried a free-text hint fed to the extractor with name-alone fallback; a second string would be two ways to say one thing (quality bar). **HARD RULES HELD:** `extraction_schemas` is already a FORCEd tenant table so the version INSERT runs under the tenant session (rule 1); it is NOT append-only, but we INSERT a new version rather than UPDATE in place to preserve history; the audit row logs field KEYS/labels/version only, never extracted VALUES (rule 6); the migration is reversible (rule 8). Renaming a field `key` orphans historical lead values under the old key — they degrade, never 500 — which the editor surfaces; editing label/type/reason/required/enum is safe for history. ### 6a. Surfaced by a decision, deliberately not decided in it

Not binding and not a row: a row is a decision, and these are the questions a decision raised and left open. They sat INSIDE the table above until 21 Aug 2026, which ended it at that line.

**OPEN, surfaced by D-74 and deliberately NOT decided there:** `docs/SURFACES.md` §2b lists the
voice on the IMMEDIATE lane and `LANES` says so, but `set_agent_voice` does not publish — so no
agent obeys the lane table, and the client screen renders "voice" under "Applies straight away".
Reconciling it means either auto-republishing (which re-voices a live line on an unrun ear test,
against OPERATIONS §2 gate 3) or amending an authoritative doc. Separately, `publish_variant`
sends the agent's CONFIGURED voice to experiment arms, so starting an experiment can move part of
the traffic while the mirror still reports "republish required" — over-reporting, which is the
safe direction, and pre-existing. Both need a decision; neither blocks anything today.

## 7. Explicitly Deferred (do not build until pulled by a client or a gate)

White-label/reseller tiers · payments-in-call · voice biometrics ·
multi-agent teams · non-India telephony · GPU inference · Temporal · separate analytics DB.

**No longer deferred: self-serve signup.** D-34/D-39 pulled it in and it ships —
`POST /v1/auth/signup`, plus the top-up intent, the server-side order route and the
payment webhook (SURFACES §2c). Server-side order creation **is** built (D-98); this line
said it was not, for a wave after it landed. What holds a client back is the credential,
not the code: the intake flag `self_serve_signup_enabled` defaults to OFF and no Razorpay
API secret is configured on any deployment, so `PaymentCapability.creates_orders` answers
False with reason `no_api_secret`. "Shipped" here means the surface and the adapter exist,
not that a client can pay today.
